raw_case_text:
A 4-year-old male with metastatic neuroblastoma underwent his second tandem autologous HCT following a conditioning regimen of melphalan, etoposide, and carboplatin. His medical history was notable for acute kidney injury secondary to cisplatin with non-functioning right kidney on imaging. His transplant course was complicated by fever and severe mucositis and mild sinusoidal obstructive syndrome (SOS). On HCT day 4 (Figure 3), he was transferred to the ICU with systemic inflammatory response and worsening respiratory distress and was found to have Lactobacillus rhamnosus sepsis and mastoiditis. Despite treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics and methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, he had worsening respiratory distress requiring endotracheal intubation on HCT day 6. He subsequently developed bloody secretions in his endotracheal tube (ETT) which led to the discontinuation of defibrotide. Bronchoscopy showed copious mucopurulent secretions in the right lower lobe which became bloody with the second aliquot on BAL and were positive for Aspergillus. He was therefore treated for presumed fungal pneumonia. Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 4 days and nebulized TXA (n-TXA) 250 mg were used for pulmonary hemorrhage control. In addition, a mean airway pressure (MAP) > 15 cm H2O was targeted to tamponade the bleed. He was transfused to maintain a hemoglobin > 7 gram/dL and a platelet count over 100 x 109/L, respectively. Hemostasis was achieved, however, he developed severe ARDS with a peak OI of 25. The ECMO liaison team initiated early joint discussions regarding ECMO candidacy at this time. The patient developed renal failure and fluid overload necessitating continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Further, he had a rising lactate dehydrogenase, refractory hypertension and thrombocytopenia, he was treated with eculizumab for suspicion of transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA).
On HCT day 24, he had an acute hypoxemic event with copious bloody secretions in his ETT. Chest radiography showed increased pulmonary opacities (Figure 4). Coagulation factors at that time included a platelet count of 97 x 109/L, and normal PT, INR, aPTT and fibrinogen levels. He was treated with intravenous TXA 1,000 mg bolus followed by 10 mg/kg/hr infusion, nebulized TXA 250 mg, and 3 doses of intrapulmonary rFVIIa (IP-rFVIIa) 50 mug/kg. Despite achieving hemostasis following IP-rFVIIa and escalation of his respiratory support to HFOV, he had progressive hypoxemia with an OI of 68. All infectious studies were negative. The added risk of mortality with multiorgan failure and SOS were discussed between the clinical and ECMO liaison teams but he was considered a candidate for ECMO due to the reversibility of his organ dysfunction. Due to his clinical acuity and high risk of death on the current support, he was transferred to the regional ECMO program. Upon arrival at the referral center, he was placed on HFOV while awaiting cannulation. Due to his small size and the presence of a femoral vascath, he was cannulated onto VA ECMO with a 14 French arterial cannula in the right carotid artery and a 15 French venous canula in the right internal jugular vein (BioMedicus Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA). He was supported with initial flows of 1.3 liters per minute (LPM), ~110 ml/kg/min, and sweep gas flow of 0.6 LPM using the Maquet CardioHelp centrifugal pump and HLS Set Advanced 7.0 Oxygenator (Maquet, Rastatt, Germany). For anticoagulation, he was placed on a bivalirudin infusion per institutional preference, titrated to maintain aPTT of 40-60 s. Given the need for systemic anticoagulation, he was treated with three additional doses of nebulized IP-rFVIIa 50 mug/kg and received IV methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day and n-TXA 250 mg every 6 h throughout his ECMO course. He had no further episodes of DAH or thromboembolic complications. CRRT was continued for fluid overload. He was maintained on higher MAP during the course of his ECMO stay. He was decannulated after 10 days of ECMO support and transferred back to the referring institution the following day.
Following return of renal function, CRRT was discontinued. He underwent tracheostomy placement 11 days following ECMO decannulation to allow gradual weaning of mean airway pressure and facilitate rehabilitation. He was weaned off mechanical ventilation support, transferred to the general medical floor under the care of the oncology team for continued radiation and chemotherapy, and successfully discharged to outpatient care on HCT day 109. He remains well 6 months following hospital discharge.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old boy with metastatic neuroblastoma developed systemic inflammatory response, worsening respiratory distress, and bloody endotracheal secretions on days +4 to +6 after his second tandem autologous hematopoietic cell transplant, followed on day +24 by life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage and refractory hypoxemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following conditioning with melphalan, etoposide, and carboplatin for his second tandem autologous HCT, the patient developed fever, severe mucositis, mild sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), and on day +4 Lactobacillus rhamnosus sepsis and mastoiditis. Intubated on day +6 for worsening respiratory distress, he developed bloody endotracheal secretions and right lower lobe Aspergillus pneumonia. Despite initial hemostasis, CRRT for renal failure, and eculizumab for transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA), he suffered massive recurrent pulmonary hemorrhage on HCT day +24 with refractory ARDS (oxygenation index 68 on HFOV) requiring emergent veno-arterial ECMO.
subjective.past_medical_history: Metastatic neuroblastoma status post second tandem autologous HCT; prior cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury with a non-functioning right kidney.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe mucositis, respiratory distress, and copious bloody endotracheal secretions.

objective.physical_examination: Intubated on day +6 with copious bloody endotracheal tube secretions, refractory hypertension (from TA-TMA), fluid overload, and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (peak OI 25 initially, worsening to OI 68 on day +24).
objective.routine_investigations: Early post-HCT blood work showed Lactobacillus rhamnosus bacteremia, rising LDH, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure requiring CRRT. At the day +24 pulmonary hemorrhage event, platelets were 97 x 10^9/L with normal PT, INR, aPTT, and fibrinogen. Chest radiographs showed progressive bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy on day +6 revealed copious mucopurulent secretions in the right lower lobe that became progressively bloody on sequential BAL aliquots, and BAL testing was positive for Aspergillus (repeat infectious studies at day +24 were negative).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Post-autologous-HCT pulmonary aspergillosis (confirmed on day +6 BAL), Lactobacillus rhamnosus sepsis/mastoiditis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, and transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA) complicated by life-threatening diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and refractory ARDS (oxygenation index 68). Treated by discontinuing defibrotide, administering antifungal and antibacterial therapy, eculizumab, CRRT, high-MAP ventilation/HFOV, intravenous and nebulized tranexamic acid (TXA), repeated intrapulmonary recombinant factor VIIa (IP-rFVIIa, 50 ug/kg), IV methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/day), and 10 days of right carotid/internal jugular veno-arterial ECMO (with bivalirudin anticoagulation), resulting in complete cessation of pulmonary hemorrhage, renal recovery, tracheostomy weaning, and hospital discharge on HCT day +109.
